newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU still has doubts on Boeing merger.
newsitem.headline: EU still has doubts on Boeing merger.

text.p: The European Commission still has serious doubts about a merger between Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp. despite U.S. Federal Trade Commission clearance for the deal, an EU source said Wednesday.
"The decision by the FTC in no way changes the serious doubts of the European Commission," the source said.
Boeing submitted various proposals to European Union antitrust officials Monday after extensive talks between the two sides.
But both sides have refused to make a specific comment about how Boeing's reply might have moved commission thinking.
European Commission coolness toward the deal contrasts with the FTC decision Tuesday to unconditionally approve the $14 billion merger.

Federal trade commissioners agreed 4-1 not to challenge any aspect of the deal, saying McDonnell Douglas was no longer a competitive force in the commercial aircraft market, an argument the EU executive disputes, the source said.

"Even if the MDC was no longer a viable competitor on a stand-alone basis, its 'competitive potential,' taken over by Boeing, would considerably strengthen Boeing's already existing dominant position in the market for large commercial aircraft," the source added.

European Commission figures put at 24 percent McDonnell Douglas's share of the global in-service aircraft fleet, a fact the source said would give Boeing access to its former rival's service contracts and spare parts market.

The EU's antitrust officials have already made clear their concerns about Boeing's exclusive deals on aircraft supply to several airlines, which they fear would increase as its market share grew from 64 percent to 70 percent after the deal.

Although the FTC took no action, it backed the EU view that Boeing's exclusive provider contracts with Delta Airlines Inc., AMR Corp.'s American Airlines and Continental Airlines Inc. were "potentially troubling."
The third area worrying the commission is the danger of spillover into Boeing's commercial aircraft businesses from its increased share of newly acquired assets in the defence and space industries.

This point concerns in particular Boeing's greater access to technology developed by publicly funded research and development in defence and space work, and the company's increased bargaining power with suppliers, the source said.
Jim Frank, Boeing vice president for European affairs, said Tuesday the company had replied to EU concerns in all three of these areas in documents submitted late Monday.
He said he was optimistic about EU regulators' reaction to the submission, supplied to meet a commission deadline.

The EU executive is set to present its thinking on the Boeing case to an advisory committee of EU national competition officials. Depending on the outcome, the full commission may vote July 23 on clearance, with or without conditions.
One Brussels-based aviation expert, who asked not to be named, doubted whether the commission would do much of substance in the face of the FTC clearance.

"What probably will happen is a lot of words which do not really mean anything but which they will play up as a bunch of concessions," said the expert, who questioned whether officials had the stomach for a full-blown confrontation between Washington and Brussels.

He predicted that measures might include an agreement to end exclusive deals, to make research funding more transparent and to allow some form of monitoring by the EU of Boeing's position in the civil aviation market.

A European aviation industry source, who also sought anonymity, disagreed, saying the danger of spillover between civil aviation and defence activities could bar EU approval of the deal without some asset sales by the merged company.
